# Why nutrition matters

> *Most deaths worldwide now come from slow, chronic diseases shaped by daily habits, and diet is
> among the largest of the risks a patient can change.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why the rise of non-communicable diseases makes prevention, and nutrition, central to
  clinical work.
- Interpret a modelled estimate of diet-related deaths as a signal of risk, not a precise count.
- Describe the six pillars of health and explain why nutrition is central to them, with two-way links
  to each of the other five.
- Explain why the overall dietary pattern predicts health better than single nutrients, and state the
  limits of the PREDIMED and DASH trials.
- Recognise nutrition counselling as a learnable clinical skill, and where its scope ends at this
  stage.
- Describe how far Singapore's population diet sits from the guidelines, and the two tools used
  in counselling (My Healthy Plate, Nutri-Grade).
:::

## Why nutrition matters at a glance {#sec-overview}

For most of medicine's history, the doctor's main concern was acute illness, injury and
infection: pneumonia, sepsis, trauma. These have not gone away, but they have been overtaken. Today,
**non-communicable diseases (NCDs)**, chronic diseases that are not passed from person to person,
cause around three-quarters of deaths worldwide, setting aside deaths from the COVID-19 pandemic
[@whoNCD2025]. The main ones are
cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory disease. NCDs are, in
large part, slow diseases of daily living, driven by a handful of modifiable behaviours: what we
eat, how much we move, whether we sleep, smoke or drink. Diet sits near the top of that list.

## The burden of non-communicable disease {#sec-burden}

The Global Burden of Disease study attributes around 11 million
deaths a year to dietary risks such as too much sodium, too few wholegrains and too little fruit,
which puts diet among the largest modifiable contributors to early death [@gbd2019diet].

::: {.callout-note}
## How precise is the 11 million figure?
The "11 million deaths" figure is a modelled estimate from observational data, and how heavily it
weights sodium is debated. The figure signals that diet is among the leading modifiable risks; it is
not a precise count of deaths.
:::

The rise of chronic disease changes the clinician's job. A clinician who can only treat the acute
crisis arrives late by definition. The larger opportunity, and the harder skill, is to prevent and
slow chronic disease, and nutrition is where that work begins.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: NCDs now cause most deaths. Why does that change the clinician's main task?
NCDs are, in large part, slow diseases of daily living, driven by modifiable behaviours such as diet. A
clinician who can only treat the acute crisis therefore arrives late, so the larger opportunity is to
prevent and slow chronic disease. Diet is among the largest modifiable contributors to early death,
which is why that preventive work begins with nutrition.
:::

## The six pillars of health {#sec-pillars}

### What the pillars are {#sec-six-pillars}

Protecting health takes more than a general instruction to "live better". It rests on a small set of
evidence-based behaviours that prevent, treat and sometimes reverse chronic disease, the **six pillars
of health** [@aclm2022comp; @lianov2010]. The pillars are used alongside drugs and surgery, never
instead of them. Each pillar names one behaviour:

Nutrition
: A predominantly whole-food, plant-rich diet.

Physical activity
: Regular movement across the week.

Restorative sleep
: Sleep of adequate quantity and quality.

Stress management
: Recognising and regulating chronic stress.

Positive social connection
: Relationships and community.

Avoidance of risky substances
: Avoiding tobacco and excess alcohol.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Healthier SG: prevention in primary care
In Singapore, this preventive, behaviour-first approach is increasingly the organising frame of
primary care, most visibly through **Healthier SG**, the national shift from reactive hospital care
toward proactive, relationship-based prevention [@mohHealthierSG].
:::

### Links between nutrition and the other pillars {#sec-hub}

Of the six pillars, nutrition is central: it connects to each of the other five, in both directions,
so a change in diet tends to shift the other pillars as well. The diagram below places nutrition at
the centre, with a two-way link to each of the other pillars.

<div data-island="pillars-hub" data-src="/diagrams/pillars-hub.yml"></div>

Nutrition links to each of the other five pillars in its own way:

- Diet and physical activity act together on weight and glucose; neither alone is as effective as
  both.
- Short sleep lowers **insulin sensitivity** (how well the body clears glucose in response to insulin)
  [@buxton2010sleep] and raises hunger and appetite, especially for energy-dense food
  [@sleepRestriction], and overall energy intake [@alkhatib2017partialsleep]. Eating late at night is
  in turn linked to poorer sleep, so the two can form a self-reinforcing loop [@crispim2011foodsleep].
- Acute and chronic stress, acting through **cortisol** (the main stress hormone), are thought to
  drive "comfort eating" of palatable, energy-dense food [@dallman2003].
- Eating is social, through family meals, communal hawker eating and festive food, so social context
  can entrench or transform a diet.
- Alcohol is itself part of the diet: it supplies empty calories and also disinhibits food choice.

One practical rule follows: start with nutrition, but plan across the pillars, because fixing the diet
often means addressing sleep and stress too.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient's diet plan keeps failing although the advice is sound. Why might the cause lie in another pillar?
Nutrition is linked to each of the other pillars in both directions. Short sleep lowers insulin
sensitivity and raises appetite and the intake of energy-dense food, and chronic stress is thought to
drive comfort eating, so problems in those pillars keep pushing intake up. Those links are why the
practical rule is to start with nutrition but plan across the pillars.
:::

## Whole dietary patterns and their evidence {#sec-patterns}

A persistent trap for patients and doctors alike is **single-nutrient reductionism**, the search for
one villain (carbohydrate, fat, gluten) or one "superfood". The evidence points instead to the
**dietary pattern**, the diet taken as a whole, which predicts health better than any isolated
nutrient [@aha2021diet]. Two of the most-studied patterns illustrate the point:

- The **Mediterranean pattern** (olive oil, nuts, legumes, fish, vegetables) lowered the risk of a
  combined measure of cardiovascular events by about 30% in relative terms in the PREDIMED trial
  [@estruch2018predimed].
- The **DASH pattern** (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension: rich in fruit, vegetables and
  low-fat dairy) lowered blood pressure meaningfully, even without weight loss or salt restriction
  [@appel1997dash].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Landmark trials come with caveats
Both results have limits (see the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd)
chapter). PREDIMED's reported result comes from a 2018 re-analysis, published after the original had
problems with how participants were assigned to groups. Its main result combined several
cardiovascular events; strokes were the largest share and showed the clearest reduction. DASH was a short controlled-feeding study that measured
blood pressure, a marker, instead of heart attacks themselves. Both are real findings that hold within
their limits, and any landmark trial is best read the same way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient wants one "superfood" to fix his diet. What follows from the evidence for the advice he should get?
The search for one superfood, or one nutrient to blame, is single-nutrient reductionism. The evidence
points to the dietary pattern, the diet taken as a whole, which predicts health better than any
isolated nutrient. The advice therefore targets his overall pattern instead of one food. The
Mediterranean and DASH patterns illustrate the point, each within the limits of its trial.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: the DASH pattern lowered blood pressure in its trial. Why does that not yet show that it prevents heart attacks?
DASH was a short controlled-feeding study that measured blood pressure, a marker, instead of heart
attacks themselves. The result is real, but it shows only what was measured: a fall in blood pressure.
Whether that fall prevents heart attacks was not tested in that trial.
:::

## Nutrition counselling as a learnable skill {#sec-skill}

Nutrition is often neglected in the clinic, largely because doctors are under-trained in it:
graduates across many countries report feeling under-prepared to give dietary advice [@crowley2019].
Yet nutrition counselling is a core competency that can be learned and examined, and diet is a
behaviour that a clinician can assess and help change [@frost2018mi]. A patient's diet is a set of
habits, shaped by environment and circumstance, that responds to skilled advice.

::: {.callout-important}
## The scope at this stage
The aim is nutritional literacy: the science, the Singapore context and the skill of advising
patients well. Training as a dietitian and prescribing protocols lie outside it at this stage.
Detailed medical nutrition therapy (a dietitian's individualised nutrition plan for a medical
condition), drug choices and disease management come later in training. Deciding when to refer is
taught later in this book, in the [*Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself*](interprofessional-referral.qmd)
chapter and the disease chapters. At this
stage, nutrition is about motivation, concepts and the clinical conversation, taught with humility
about what the evidence does and does not show.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is nutrition often neglected in the clinic, and why can that change?
Doctors are under-trained in nutrition: graduates across many countries report feeling under-prepared
to give dietary advice. The gap is not fixed, because nutrition counselling is a competency that can
be learned, and a patient's diet is a set of habits, shaped by environment and circumstance,
that responds to skilled advice.
:::

## Why should a doctor care about food? {#sec-close}

NCDs now cause most deaths, and diet is among their leading modifiable risks. Unlike much of
medicine, diet is something the patient can change, so advising on it is part of the doctor's job.
Diet is linked in both directions to activity, sleep, stress, social life and alcohol, so improving
it can move the other pillars too, and advising on it is a clinical skill that can be learned and
examined.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Diet-related disease is a declared national priority. The **War on Diabetes**, launched in 2016,
treats diabetes as a population-scale problem [@mohWarOnDiabetes]: roughly 1 in 3 Singaporeans has a
lifetime risk of diabetes, with higher risk among Malay and Indian residents.

The National Nutrition Survey 2022 shows how far the population diet sits from the guidelines
[@mohNNS2022]:

| Finding (NNS 2022) | What it means |
|---|---|
| Only ~4% of staples eaten are wholegrain | A quality gap (refined rice and noodles dominate) |
| ~9 in 10 residents exceed the WHO sodium limit | Most sodium comes from sauces, broths and food eaten out |

Singapore translates the guidelines into two tools that clinicians use in counselling:

My Healthy Plate
: The "quarter, quarter, half" plate: ¼ wholegrains, ¼ protein, ½ fruit and vegetables
  [@hpbHealthyPlate].

Nutri-Grade
: The A–D front-of-pack grade on drinks, by sugar and saturated fat, familiar from the labels on
  *teh tarik* and bubble tea [@hpbNutriGrade].

These tools keep advice concrete and local, as in two everyday swaps:

::: {.example}
A *cai png* (economy rice) plate becomes "two veg, one protein, less gravy", and a Grade-D drink
becomes *kopi-o kosong* or plain water.
:::
